messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mohammad is a 34-year-old Middle Eastern man who works as a publisher and is married. The traumatic event that continues to haunt him occurred when his young daughter was in a severe car accident. The incident left her with life-threatening injuries, and Mohammad found himself in the emergency room, feeling utterly helpless as he watched medical professionals rush around her. Since then, Mohammad has experienced several triggers that have made it difficult for him to lead a normal life. One of the most potent triggers is feeling vulnerable or naked; this sensation of helplessness often brings back fragments of memory from the accident and the subsequent hours in the hospital. Another trigger involves riding public transport, particularly buses, which he now associates with feelings of exhaustion and vulnerability. Mohammad’s constant vigilance has led him to develop a heightened sense of threat perception. He frequently scans people's faces and body language for signs of danger and notices potential weapons or dangerous objects around him in any environment. This behavior is driven by his fragmented memories of the event, which come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together. When he does recall specific details, he hears sounds from that day—sirens wailing and doctors shouting—in his head. The trauma has also led to a recurring memory loop where moments from the accident replay over and over again in his mind, often triggered by being on public transport or feeling extremely tired. These fragmented memories of the event are like a film that plays repeatedly, causing him significant distress. The vivid auditory recall only intensifies his anxiety and sense of threat. Mohammad’s fear of unfamiliar places stems from his inability to assess danger accurately when he feels vulnerable or exhausted. Riding the bus often leads to feelings of exhaustion, which in turn triggers fragmented memories and an overwhelming sense of threat. His heightened vigilance has caused him to avoid public transport altogether and limit his visits to new or unfamiliar locations. His occupation as a publisher requires frequent travel for meetings with authors and attending book fairs. This work environment makes it challenging for Mohammad to manage his symptoms, as he often finds himself in situations that can trigger his anxiety. For example, being on the bus to an out-of-town meeting often leaves him feeling exhausted and vulnerable, which triggers intrusive memories of the accident. The cycle has become self-reinforcing over time. The fragmented nature of his memories ensures that any small detail or sensation—such as hearing a siren or seeing a group of people who look threatening—can trigger intense anxiety and flashbacks. This makes it increasingly difficult for Mohammad to function in his daily life, leading him to avoid more situations where he feels unsafe. What frightens Mohammad most is the fear of losing control again, just like when he was helpless watching doctors rush around his injured daughter. He fears that this anxiety will not only affect his work but also strain his marriage and family life. Despite these challenges, Mohammad hopes for a way to regain some sense of normalcy and peace in his daily life. His recent decision to seek help comes from the realization that avoiding triggers is no longer manageable, particularly given his demanding job. He is seeking support to better cope with his symptoms and find ways to navigate through his daily routines without being overwhelmed by fear and intrusive memories.
